history.heading: Peoples of the Nile
paragraphs: South Sudan, in the Upper Nile region, has long been home to Nilotic peoples such as the Dinka, Nuer and Shilluk, as well as the Azande and many others, mainly pastoralists and farmers. In the 19th century the region was raided for slaves and ivory by traders from the north and by Egyptian-Ottoman forces.

history.heading: Anglo-Egyptian rule and civil wars
paragraphs: Under Anglo-Egyptian rule from 1899, the south was administered separately from the north, with Christian missions and little development. When Sudan became independent in 1956, southerners feared domination by the Arab and Muslim north.

The First Sudanese Civil War (1955–1972) ended with southern autonomy, but war resumed in 1983 when the government imposed Islamic law. The Second Civil War, led by John Garang's Sudan People's Liberation Army, killed around two million people. The 2005 Comprehensive Peace Agreement provided for a referendum.

history.heading: Independence and conflict
paragraphs: In January 2011, nearly 99 percent of southerners voted for independence, and South Sudan became the world's newest country on 9 July 2011. In December 2013 a power struggle between President Salva Kiir (Dinka) and Vice-President Riek Machar (Nuer) erupted into civil war, killing an estimated 400,000 people. A 2018 peace deal created a unity government, but elections have been repeatedly postponed. In 2025 Machar was arrested and charged, raising fears of renewed war.

culture.heading: Peoples and traditions
paragraphs: South Sudan has over 60 ethnic groups. English is the official language, and Juba Arabic is widely spoken. Most people are Christian or follow traditional religions.

Cattle are central to the culture and economy of many groups, used for dowries and status. Ritual scarification and songs dedicated to cattle are traditions. Basketball is popular, and the national team qualified for the 2024 Olympics.

politics.heading: Fragile state
paragraphs: South Sudan is a presidential republic led by Salva Kiir since independence. The transitional government has struggled to implement the peace agreement, unify armed forces or hold elections. Ethnic violence, corruption and humanitarian crises persist. A UN peacekeeping mission is present.

economy.heading: Oil and poverty
paragraphs: Oil provides nearly all exports and government revenue, but it must be exported through pipelines across Sudan, and the war in Sudan disrupted them. Most people depend on subsistence farming and herding, and South Sudan is one of the poorest countries in the world, with widespread hunger and frequent flooding. The currency is the South Sudanese pound.
